To power the Sylvania F4T5/CW bulb shown in your photo, you need a specific electrical setup because fluorescent tubes cannot be plugged directly into a wall outlet or a simple battery.

This is a 4-watt, T5 miniature linear fluorescent bulb (6 inches long) with a G5 bi-pin base. Here is what you need to make it work:

1. The Essential Components

  • Ballast: This is the most critical part. It regulates the current and provides the initial high-voltage "kick" to start the lamp. For this specific bulb, you need a 4-watt T5 ballast (magnetic or electronic).
  • Starter (if using a Magnetic Ballast): Older magnetic ballasts require a small cylindrical "starter" (typically an FS-5 model for this wattage) to preheat the filaments.
  • Sockets (Tombstones): You need two G5 miniature bi-pin lamp holders to hold the pins at each end of the tube.

2. Common Powering Methods

Depending on your project, you have a few options:

  • AC Power (Home Use): Buy an under-cabinet light fixture designed for 6-inch T5 bulbs. This is the safest way, as the ballast and sockets are already wired inside a housing.
  • DC Power (Portable/Battery): These bulbs were commonly used in camping lanterns (like Coleman models) and emergency lights. These devices use a small inverter circuit to convert battery power (6V or 12V) into the high-frequency AC the bulb needs.
  • DIY / Electronics: If you are building a custom setup, you can buy a dedicated "1-lamp F4T5 electronic ballast." Modern electronic ballasts are easier to wire because they don't require a separate starter.

⚠️ Important Safety Notes

  • Mercury: This bulb contains a small amount of mercury (indicated by the (Hg) symbol on the glass). If it breaks, do not vacuum; ventilate the room and use damp paper towels to pick up the fragments.
  • Voltage: The ballast outputs high voltage. Never touch the pins or sockets while the power is on.
  • Don't "Direct Wire": If you connect the pins directly to 120V AC without a ballast, the bulb will likely pop or trip your breaker immediately.

When choosing a ballast for your F4T5 bulb, the "other one" you're referring to is an electronic ballast. While both perform the same basic function—regulating electricity to the bulb—they do so using very different technology.

Comparison: Magnetic vs. Electronic Ballasts

FeatureMagnetic BallastElectronic Ballast
OperationUses heavy copper coils and a transformer at 60Hz.Uses solid-state circuitry at 20,000Hz+.
StartingUsually requires a separate starter (FS-5).Starts instantly without a separate part.
NoiseCan produce a noticeable hum or buzz.Virtually silent operation.
Light QualityMay have a visible flicker at low frequencies.Flicker-free, stable light output.
EfficiencyHeavier, runs hotter, and uses more power.Lighter, runs cooler, and is more energy-efficient.

Which one should you choose?

For your specific Sylvania 4W bulb, I recommend going with an electronic ballast.

The Robertson RSZ108T5120-WT/B is a top choice for DIYers. It is an electronic, rapid-start ballast that eliminates the need for a starter, making your wiring much simpler. It’s also very compact, which is perfect if you’re building a small custom fixture or a portable lamp.

If you are replacing a ballast in an older, vintage fixture and want to keep it original, the Robertson 04827P Magnetic Ballast is the way to go. Just remember that you will also need to ensure your FS-5 starter is in good working order for the bulb to fire up.

Summary: Unless you are doing a period-accurate restoration, electronic ballasts are the modern standard because they are quieter, more efficient, and easier to install.
